title: The C# language
blurb: Value vs reference types, LINQ, records, nullability, async. Written for someone who already knows JavaScript.

questions.q: What is the key difference between a value type and a reference type?
choices: Value types are immutable once created, while reference types can always be changed in place
Value types always live on the stack, while reference types always live on the managed heap
A value-type variable holds the data itself; a reference-type variable holds a reference to it
Reference types cannot be null, while value types default to null until they are assigned
questions.why: Assigning a struct copies it; assigning a class copies the reference, so both names see the same object. "Stack vs heap" is the tempting answer but it is an implementation detail and often false: a struct field inside a class lives on the heap. `int`, `bool`, `DateTime`, enums and structs are value types; classes, arrays, strings and delegates are reference types.
questions.asked: The classic first C# question, and it explains a whole category of surprising behaviour.

questions.q: What is the difference between `struct`, `class` and `record`?
choices: record is a struct with methods, class is a reference type, and struct cannot have methods
struct is a value type, class a reference type, and record adds value equality and `with`
class and record compile to the same type, and struct is a class that the GC ignores
struct and record are both value types, and class is the only reference type of the three
questions.why: `record` is a reference type by default (`record struct` is the value-type form), which is why "struct and record are value types" is wrong. Its win is generated Equals, GetHashCode, ToString and non-destructive mutation, which suits DTOs and domain values. Structs can have methods, constructors and properties.
questions.asked: Checks you can pick the right kind of type for a DTO, an entity and a small value such as Money.

choices: It does not compile
questions.why: `List<T>` is a class, so `a` and `b` reference the same list, and adding through `b` is visible through `a`. Same lesson as JavaScript object references: the syntax differs, the trap does not. `1` is what you would get if assignment copied the list, which only happens for structs.
questions.asked: A warm-up that confirms reference semantics before the harder questions.

questions.q: When does a LINQ query actually execute?
choices: Immediately, on the line where the query expression is written
When the enclosing method returns, so the results are ready for its caller
When it is enumerated: by foreach, ToList, First, Count and similar calls
On a background thread as soon as it is defined, then awaited on first use
questions.why: Deferred execution means the query can run twice, or observe changes made to the source after it was defined. Against a database it also means the whole chain composes into one SQL statement until you materialise it. Nothing runs in the background: enumeration is synchronous unless you use the async operators.
questions.asked: Nearly guaranteed. The follow-up is the IQueryable/IEnumerable question.

questions.q: What is wrong here, against a database?
choices: Where cannot follow ToList, so this fails to compile against a List<User>
Take must come before Where, or the whole table is sorted before limiting
Nothing: EF Core sees the whole chain and still turns it into one SQL query
ToList() runs first and pulls every user into memory before the filter runs
questions.why: Once you call ToList the query stops being IQueryable, and everything after it runs in your process over the full table. EF cannot see past a materialisation. Move ToList to the end and the filter and limit become SQL WHERE and TOP/LIMIT. It compiles fine, which is why the bug survives review.
questions.asked: A very common real bug, and the reason to know the difference between the two interfaces.

questions.q: What do nullable reference types (C# 8+) give you?
choices: Runtime null checks inserted before every member access, which throw ArgumentNullException
Compile-time warnings when a possibly-null reference is dereferenced (`string?` vs `string`)
A guarantee that NullReferenceException cannot happen in code that compiles cleanly
Automatic null coalescing, so that a null string is read back as an empty string
questions.why: They are annotations plus flow analysis, erased at runtime, much like TypeScript's strictNullChecks. So there is no guarantee: data from JSON, reflection or code with warnings suppressed can still be null. The `!` null-forgiving operator silences a warning without checking anything.
questions.asked: A strong answer names the gaps (deserialisation, `!`) rather than claiming NREs are gone.

questions.q: What does `async void` do, and when is it acceptable?
choices: It is the standard return type for async methods with no result, like void in sync code
Its exceptions cannot be caught by the caller and can crash the process; only for event handlers
It is required for fire-and-forget work, because an async Task must always be awaited
It runs the method synchronously to the end, so it suits short handlers that must never yield
questions.why: `async Task` gives the caller something to await and a place for the exception to surface. `async void` rethrows on the synchronization context (or the thread pool), where nothing can catch it. Event handlers are the exception because their signature is fixed. Fire-and-forget still wants a Task you can observe.
questions.asked: A standard .NET question. The correct answer includes "except for event handlers".

questions.q: What is the danger of `.Result` or `.Wait()` on a Task?
choices: It always throws, because a task result can be read only by awaiting it
It silently swallows any exception and returns the default value instead
It is a safe way to run async code synchronously in any kind of application
It blocks the thread, and can deadlock where a synchronization context exists
questions.why: Classic deadlock: the continuation needs the context thread, which is blocked waiting for the task. ASP.NET Core has no such context so it deadlocks less, but it still ties up a thread-pool thread and can starve the pool under load. Exceptions are not swallowed: they arrive wrapped in AggregateException.
questions.asked: Tests whether you understand "async all the way" rather than reciting it.

questions.q: What is the difference between `IEnumerable<T>` and `IQueryable<T>`?
choices: IQueryable is the newer name for IEnumerable, and both behave the same when enumerated
IEnumerable works only on arrays and lists, while IQueryable works on any collection type
IQueryable builds an expression tree that a provider translates; IEnumerable runs in memory
IQueryable executes as soon as it is created, while IEnumerable waits for its enumeration
questions.why: It decides where the work happens. A `Where` on IQueryable becomes part of an expression tree that EF translates into a SQL WHERE clause; on IEnumerable it is a C# loop over rows already fetched. Both are deferred, so "executes immediately" is wrong for either.
questions.asked: The follow-up to deferred execution; interviewers want "where does the filter run".

questions.q: What does `using var stream = File.OpenRead(path);` do?
choices: Imports the stream type's namespace for the rest of the file, like a using directive
Disposes the stream when the enclosing scope ends, even if an exception is thrown
Makes the variable readonly, so it cannot be reassigned later in the method
Opens the file asynchronously and closes it when the garbage collector runs
questions.why: A using declaration calls Dispose at the end of the enclosing block, in a hidden finally, so file handles, sockets and connections are released promptly. The garbage collector would release them eventually, which is too late for a file lock or a connection pool. The `using` directive at the top of a file is an unrelated feature with the same keyword.
questions.asked: Deterministic cleanup is a basic .NET expectation; forgetting it causes connection-pool exhaustion.

questions.q: What is the difference between an interface and an abstract class?
choices: Interfaces can hold per-instance state, while abstract classes can hold only methods
Abstract classes cannot have constructors, while interfaces can declare constructors for implementers
They are interchangeable, except that interface calls are faster at runtime
A class implements many interfaces but one base class; only the latter holds instance state
questions.why: Use an interface for a capability ("this can be saved") and an abstract class for shared implementation in a real is-a hierarchy. Since C# 8 interfaces can have default methods and static members, but still no instance fields, so state and single inheritance still decide it. Abstract classes can and often do have constructors.
questions.asked: A guaranteed OOP question. The strong answer picks a concrete example.

questions.q: What does the `?.` and `??` combination do here?
questions.code: var name = user?.Profile?.DisplayName ?? "Anonymous";
choices: Throws NullReferenceException if user is null, but handles a null Profile
Returns an empty string when any link is null, ignoring the fallback value
Short-circuits to null if any link is null, then substitutes "Anonymous"
Checks only the first link for null, so a null Profile still throws
questions.why: Each `?.` stops the chain and yields null as soon as its left side is null, and `??` replaces a null result with the fallback. The semantics are identical to JavaScript's optional chaining and nullish coalescing, one of the easiest transfers between the two languages.
questions.asked: A quick check for JavaScript developers that the familiar operators behave the same way.

questions.q: What is boxing?
choices: Wrapping a value type in a heap object when it is treated as object or an interface
Encapsulating a public field behind a property, so callers use a getter and setter
Copying a struct into a field of a class, which moves it from the stack to the heap
Wrapping a method call in a try/catch block so that its exceptions are contained
questions.why: Boxing allocates a new object and copies the value into it; unboxing copies it back out. A struct stored as a class field is on the heap too, but inline, with no separate object, so that is not boxing. In a hot loop, boxing through non-generic collections or `object` parameters is a real allocation cost, which is one reason generics exist.
questions.asked: An allocation-awareness question; the follow-up is how generics avoid it.

questions.q: What does `yield return` do?
choices: It returns early from the loop, like break, but keeps the last value it computed so far
It returns all the values at once as a List that the compiler builds for you
It returns a Task, so the caller has to await each value the method produces
It builds a lazy iterator: values are produced one at a time as the caller enumerates
questions.why: The compiler turns the method into a state machine that resumes where it left off each time the caller asks for the next item. It streams results without building a list, and the method body does not run at all until enumeration starts, so argument validation in it is also deferred.
questions.asked: Connects to deferred execution; the deferred-validation gotcha is the senior follow-up.

questions.q: What is the difference between `String.Empty`, `null` and `""` for a string?
choices: null is no string at all; String.Empty and "" are the same zero-length string
All three are equivalent, because string comparison always treats null as empty
String.Empty is null internally, while "" is a real zero-length string
null and "" are the same value, while String.Empty is a separate object
questions.why: `"" == String.Empty` is true and both have length 0, while calling `.Length` on null throws. `==` does not treat null as empty. For user input you almost always want `string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace`, which covers null, empty and a string of spaces in one call.
questions.asked: Leads straight to how you validate form input, which is the real point.

questions.q: Which collection gives fast lookup of an item by its key?
choices: `List<T>` searched with Find, which is O(1) because lists are indexed
`Dictionary<TKey, TValue>`, which hashes keys for O(1) average lookup
`SortedList<TKey, TValue>`, which beats hashing for every lookup
`Queue<T>`, which keeps arrival order so that lookup stays constant
questions.why: A dictionary hashes the key to find its bucket directly. A List is O(1) only by position; finding an item by a property means scanning, O(n). SortedList uses binary search, O(log n). `HashSet<T>` is the equivalent when you only need membership. It is the C# version of "Map or array?".
questions.asked: Checks you choose collections by access pattern, which matters in every data-shaping job.

questions.q: What does a record's `with` expression do?
questions.code: var updated = user with { Email = "new@example.com" };
choices: Mutates the original record in place, which its init-only setter allows
Creates a copy with Email changed, leaving the original record untouched
Creates a mutable view that shares all of its storage with the original record
Merges two records, taking Email from one and the rest from the other
questions.why: Non-destructive mutation: the compiler clones the record and sets the listed properties on the clone. It is the same idea as `{ ...user, email }` in JavaScript, but type-checked. The copy is shallow, so a list property is shared between the original and the copy.
questions.asked: Checks you are comfortable with immutable models, and the shallow-copy detail is the follow-up.

questions.q: By the usual .NET guidance, when should you throw an exception rather than return a failure result?
choices: Always, because exceptions are the idiomatic C# way to report any failure at all
Never, because a Result type is always faster and clearer than throwing an exception
For unexpected conditions like bugs or a broken dependency, not for failed validation
Only in library code, because application code should catch and log every error
questions.why: "User not found" and "invalid input" are expected outcomes of a request and belong in the return type (or a 400/404). A malformed connection string or a dead database is exceptional and should throw. Exceptions are also expensive when thrown in a loop, which is why using them for control flow is discouraged.
questions.asked: An opinion question that mirrors the TypeScript Result discussion; the strong answer gives one example of each.

questions.q: What does a `CancellationToken` do in an async method?
choices: Lets a caller abort the running task from outside, stopping its thread immediately
Sets a timeout on the request automatically, using the server default of 30 seconds
Rolls back any database transaction the method opened when the caller disconnects
Lets a caller signal that the work should stop, and the method stops cooperatively
questions.why: Cancellation is cooperative: the method must check the token or pass it down, and nothing is killed from outside. ASP.NET Core gives you `HttpContext.RequestAborted` (or a `CancellationToken` parameter), so passing it into database calls means a user who navigates away stops burning server work.
questions.asked: Checks whether you pass tokens through in real code; many codebases forget.

questions.q: What is pattern matching used for in modern C#?
choices: Branching on shape and value: type and property patterns, and exhaustive switch expressions
Matching strings against regular expressions, as a faster built-in replacement for the Regex class
Formatting values into strings by matching placeholders, as interpolated strings do
Reflecting over attributes at runtime to pick which method should handle a request
questions.why: `result switch { Success s => ..., NotFound => ..., _ => ... }` is C#'s answer to a discriminated union. The compiler warns on a switch expression that misses cases, which is the exhaustiveness check. It has nothing to do with regular expressions despite the name.
questions.asked: Modern C# style; a strong answer shows a switch expression over a result type.

questions.q: What does an extension method let you do?
choices: Override a sealed method on a type from another assembly, replacing its behaviour
Add new fields to an existing class, so that each instance can store extra data
Add a callable method to an existing type without modifying or inheriting from it
Change which interfaces a type implements at runtime, for example to mock it
questions.why: It is a static method whose first parameter is `this T value`, called with instance syntax. All of LINQ is extension methods on IEnumerable<T>. It cannot access private state, add fields or override anything: it is syntax, not inheritance, and an instance method with the same signature always wins.
questions.asked: Explains how LINQ works, and the "instance method wins" rule catches people out.

questions.q: What is the difference between `==` and `.Equals()` for a class?
choices: `==` always compares values, while `Equals` always compares references
`Equals` compares values, while `==` compares references unless the type is a struct
By default both compare references; records and string override both for values
They are identical in every case, because `==` compiles to a call to `Equals`
questions.why: `==` is a static operator chosen at compile time; `Equals` is virtual and chosen at runtime. For a plain class both default to reference equality, which is why two structurally identical instances are not equal and why records exist. A type can overload one without the other, which is a classic bug.
questions.asked: Checks the difference between static operators and virtual methods, which also explains equality bugs in collections.

questions.q: Which of these makes the compiler reject any code that assigns to an instance's fields after construction?
choices: A `readonly` field that holds a class instance, which freezes that object's fields too
An `in` parameter of a class type, which makes the object's fields read-only in the method
Declaring the type as a `readonly struct`, which requires every field to be readonly
A `const` field, which can hold any type, including an instance of your own class
questions.why: A `readonly struct` makes every field readonly, so no member, including its own methods, can assign one. A `readonly` field only stops the field being reassigned; the object it points to stays mutable. `in` passes a read-only reference, which protects a struct's fields but not a class instance's. `const` is only for compile-time constants such as numbers and strings.
questions.asked: Three meanings of "read-only" in C#; the interviewer wants to hear which one is shallow.

questions.q: What is the purpose of a generic constraint like `where T : class, new()`?
choices: It improves performance, because the JIT then compiles one shared version for every T
It makes T nullable, so the method may return null for T without any warning
It is required on every generic method, since an unconstrained T is unusable
It limits T, so the method can rely on it being a class with a public constructor
questions.why: Without a constraint you can do very little with T. `where T : IEntity` lets you read `item.Id`; `new()` lets you write `new T()`; `class` allows null checks and `as`. Unconstrained generics are legal and common (`List<T>`). It is the same idea as `extends` in a TypeScript generic.
questions.asked: Generic repositories and helpers come up in most .NET codebases; constraints are how they compile.

questions.q: What is the difference between the two delegate types here?
choices: `Func` returns a value, its last type argument; `Action` returns nothing
`Func` is for lambdas, while `Action` is for pointing at existing named methods
`Action` runs asynchronously, while `Func` runs on the calling thread
`Func` can take parameters, while `Action` must always take none
questions.why: `Func<T1, …, TResult>` and `Action<T1, …>` are the built-in generic delegate types: the difference is only the return value. Both accept lambdas or method groups, both can take up to 16 parameters, and both run synchronously. They are what LINQ and minimal API handlers take, which is why they matter.
questions.asked: A JavaScript developer passes functions around constantly; this checks you can type them in C#.

questions.q: Why do C# classes expose `public string Name { get; set; }` rather than a public field?
choices: Public fields are not allowed in C#, so a property is the only way to expose data
A property can gain logic later without breaking callers, and serialisers use it
Auto-properties are stored more compactly in memory than fields of the same type
Auto-properties are thread-safe, while a public field needs an explicit lock
questions.why: Changing a field to a property later is a binary-breaking change, while a property can add validation or change notification without touching callers. System.Text.Json and model binding work with public properties and ignore fields by default. An auto-property is a hidden field plus accessors: same memory, no locking.
questions.asked: Basic C# idiom; the serialiser detail explains a common "why is my JSON empty" bug.

questions.q: What is wrong with `throw ex;` in this handler?
choices: It wraps the exception in an AggregateException, which callers do not expect
It resets the stack trace to this line, hiding where the error really happened
It logs the exception a second time, because `throw ex` calls the logger again
Nothing: `throw ex;` and `throw;` compile to exactly the same IL instruction
questions.why: `throw ex;` throws the object again as if it started here, so the stack trace no longer shows the line inside SaveAsync that failed. `throw;` rethrows the current exception with its original trace. If you need to add context, throw a new exception with the original as InnerException.
questions.asked: A code-review classic; it shows whether you have debugged from production stack traces.

questions.q: Why is `DateTimeOffset` usually the safer type for timestamps a web API stores and returns?
choices: It stores times with finer precision than DateTime, down to single nanoseconds
It converts every value to the server's local time zone automatically on read
It carries its UTC offset, so the instant it represents is never ambiguous
It is a reference type, so it can be null without declaring it as nullable
questions.why: A `DateTime` has a Kind (Utc, Local or Unspecified), and values from JSON or a database often arrive as Unspecified, so the same value can mean different instants on different servers. `DateTimeOffset` records the offset with the value. Both are structs with 100 ns ticks. Storing UTC `DateTime` consistently also works, but it is a convention the type does not enforce.
questions.asked: Time-zone bugs are common in CRUD apps; the interviewer wants to hear "store an unambiguous instant".

questions.q: Why is this loop slow for 100,000 lines?
choices: Each += interns the new string in a global pool, and that pool lookup is slow
Each += converts the whole string to a char array and back, doubling its size
The compiler cannot optimise string loops, so the JIT is disabled for this whole method
Strings are immutable, so each += copies everything built so far into a new string
questions.why: A string can never change, so every `+=` allocates a new string and copies all the previous characters: the total work grows with the square of the length. `StringBuilder` appends into a growable buffer, and `string.Join("\n", lines)` does it in one pass. Runtime strings are not interned unless you ask.
questions.asked: An old question that still filters people who have never looked at allocation behaviour.

questions.q: What does `protected internal` mean on a member?
choices: Accessible only from derived classes that are also in the same assembly
Accessible from the same assembly, or from derived classes in any assembly
Accessible from anywhere like public, but hidden from other projects' IntelliSense
Accessible only inside the declaring class and any of its nested types
questions.why: `protected internal` is the union: either condition grants access. The intersection (derived and in the same assembly) is `private protected`, which is the tempting wrong answer. `internal` alone is the usual way to hide implementation types inside a class library while keeping them public within it.
questions.asked: Rarely used, often confused; it tests precise knowledge of the access-modifier rules.

questions.q: What does this print?
choices: 10, because structs are passed to methods by reference
1, because the method received its own copy of the struct
0, because the struct is reset when the method returns
A compile error, because a struct field cannot be assigned
questions.why: A struct argument is copied into the parameter, so `Move` changes its private copy and `pt` keeps X = 1. Passing by reference needs the `ref` keyword at both the declaration and the call site. If `Point` were a class, the method would mutate the shared object and print 10.
questions.asked: Checks that you can predict copy semantics before they cause a lost-update bug in real code.

questions.q: Why does the second line fail to compile?
choices: The list indexer returns a copy of the struct, so assigning to its field would be lost
List<T> is read-only for value types, so no element can be changed after it is added
Struct fields are implicitly readonly, so X can only be set inside a constructor
The indexer returns a nullable Point?, so X must be reached through the ?. operator
questions.why: `List<T>`'s indexer is a method that returns the element by value, so `points[0]` is a temporary copy; the compiler rejects the assignment (CS1612) because it would silently vanish. With an array, `arr[0].X = 5` works because array elements are variables. The fix is to copy out, modify, and write back, or to use a class.
questions.asked: A real compile error people hit when they use mutable structs as DTOs, and it shows whether you understand that indexers are methods.

questions.q: What is the difference between `ref` and `out` parameters?
choices: `ref` passes a copy of the variable, while `out` passes the variable itself to the method
`ref` works only with value types, while `out` works only with reference types
`ref` needs the caller to initialise the variable; `out` needs the method to assign it
`ref` lets the method read the argument, while `out` makes it read-only for the method
questions.why: Both pass the caller's variable by reference. `ref` requires definite assignment before the call, so the method may read it; `out` does not, but the method must assign it before returning, which is why it suits `TryParse`-style APIs. Both work with any type.
questions.asked: Comes up whenever you explain the Try pattern; a strong answer mentions `int.TryParse(s, out var n)`.

questions.q: What does this print?
choices: ANN, because ToUpper converts the string in place
ann, because ToUpper returns a new string and the result is discarded
A compile error, because the return value of ToUpper must be used
Ann, because ToUpper only capitalises the first character
questions.why: Strings are immutable; every method that looks like it edits one returns a new string. Here the result is thrown away, so `name` is unchanged. You need `name = name.ToUpper();`. Ignoring the return value is legal C#, though analysers can warn about it.
questions.asked: A quick check that a JavaScript developer's string intuition carries across, and a lead-in to StringBuilder.

questions.q: In C#, what does `==` compare when both operands are of type `string`?
choices: The references, so two equal strings built at runtime compare as false
The hash codes, so strings with colliding hashes can compare as true
The characters, case-insensitively, using the current culture's rules
The characters, ordinally, because string overloads the == operator
questions.why: `string` overloads `==` to call `string.Equals`, an ordinal, case-sensitive comparison of the characters, so two separately built strings with the same text are equal. Reference comparison only happens if the static types are `object`. Case-insensitive comparison needs `string.Equals(a, b, StringComparison.OrdinalIgnoreCase)`.
questions.asked: Java developers expect reference comparison here; interviewers use it to see whether you know C# strings behave like values.

questions.q: What is `var` in C#?
choices: A dynamically typed variable whose type can change on each assignment
An implicitly typed local whose static type the compiler infers once
A variable of type object that is cast back automatically when read
A function-scoped variable, the way `var` works in JavaScript
questions.why: `var` is compile-time inference: `var n = 5;` makes `n` an `int` forever and `n = "x"` fails to compile. It is only allowed for locals with an initialiser. Runtime typing is `dynamic`, which is a different feature; C# locals are always block-scoped.
questions.asked: JavaScript developers often assume `var` is loose; saying "static type, inferred" is the whole answer.

questions.q: What is the difference between `var` and `dynamic`?
choices: `var` is resolved by the compiler; `dynamic` defers member lookup to runtime
`var` can hold any type; `dynamic` only holds types deriving from object
`var` is inferred at runtime; `dynamic` is inferred by the compiler
`var` boxes value types; `dynamic` keeps them unboxed on the stack
questions.why: `var` produces an ordinary statically typed local. `dynamic` switches off compile-time checking: member access is bound at runtime, so a typo becomes a `RuntimeBinderException` instead of a compile error. It is rare in application code, mostly for COM interop or ad-hoc JSON.
questions.asked: Tests whether you understand what the compiler is protecting you from; strong answers say they almost never use dynamic.

questions.q: What is the difference between `const` and `readonly` fields?
choices: `const` can be set in a constructor; `readonly` must be set where it is declared
`const` is a compile-time literal baked into callers; `readonly` is set at runtime
`const` applies only to strings; `readonly` applies to every type
`const` is per-instance; `readonly` is always static and shared
questions.why: A `const` must be a compile-time constant (numbers, strings, bools, null) and is implicitly static; the compiler copies its value into every place that uses it. A `readonly` field is assigned at runtime, in its initialiser or a constructor, and can hold any type, such as a `TimeSpan` or a list.
questions.asked: A basics question; the follow-up is why a public const can bite you across assemblies.

questions.q: Library A exposes `public const int MaxItems = 50;`. App B uses it. You change A to 100 and redeploy only A's DLL. What does B use?
choices: 100, because B reads the constant from A's assembly every time it runs
100 after the first restart, once B's JIT cache has been cleared
A MissingFieldException, because the constant's value no longer matches
50, because the compiler copied the literal into B when B was built
questions.why: Constants are inlined at compile time, so B's IL contains the literal 50 until B is recompiled. A `public static readonly` field is read from A at runtime and would pick up 100. That is why values that might change belong in `static readonly` or configuration, not `const`.
questions.asked: Separates people who know what const compiles to from those who treat it as a fancier readonly.

questions.q: What does `Console.WriteLine(7 / 2);` print?
questions.why: Both operands are `int`, so C# performs integer division and truncates toward zero, giving 3. Unlike JavaScript there is no single number type. Make one operand floating point, `7 / 2.0` or `7m / 2`, to get 3.5.
questions.asked: Catches JavaScript habits early; the same bug appears in average and percentage calculations.

questions.q: Why do you use `decimal` rather than `double` for money in C#?
choices: decimal is a base-10 type, so values like 0.10 are stored exactly
decimal has a much larger range, so totals never overflow
decimal arithmetic is faster because it runs on dedicated hardware
decimal rounds every result to two places, which suits currency
questions.why: `double` is binary floating point, so 0.1 and 0.2 cannot be represented exactly and sums drift. `decimal` stores a 96-bit integer and a power-of-ten scale, so cents are exact. It is slower than double and has a smaller range, and it does not round to two places for you.
questions.asked: Every CRUD app with prices or invoices needs this; a strong answer also maps it to `decimal(18,2)` in SQL.

questions.q: What does this print?
choices: True True
False False
True False
False True
questions.why: In binary floating point 0.1 + 0.2 is 0.30000000000000004, so the double comparison is False. The `m` suffix makes decimal literals, which hold 0.1 and 0.2 exactly, so the decimal sum equals 0.3m. Compare doubles with a tolerance rather than `==`.
questions.asked: The same floating point trap as JavaScript, used to check you know C# has a decimal escape hatch.

questions.q: What does this print in a default project (no `checked` setting)?
choices: An OverflowException is thrown
2147483647, because the value saturates
questions.why: Integer arithmetic is unchecked by default, so the value wraps around to `int.MinValue`. Wrap in `checked(...)` or enable `<CheckForOverflowUnderflow>` to get an `OverflowException`. There is no promotion to a wider type and no saturation.
questions.asked: Silent wraparound corrupts counters and totals; interviewers want to hear about `checked` or using `long`.

questions.q: What does this print?
choices: False, 0, then 0 again
False, then a NullReferenceException
False, 0, then an InvalidOperationException
null, 0, then a NullReferenceException
questions.why: `int?` is `Nullable<int>`, a struct with a flag and a value. `HasValue` is false and `GetValueOrDefault()` returns 0, but reading `.Value` on an empty nullable throws `InvalidOperationException`, not a NullReferenceException, because there is no reference to dereference.
questions.asked: Nullable value types show up in every optional database column; knowing which exception you get helps you read logs.

questions.q: What does `settings.Theme ??= "light";` do?
choices: Assigns "light" to Theme only when Theme is currently null
Assigns "light" to Theme when Theme is null or an empty string
Compares Theme with "light" and returns true when either is null
Throws when Theme is null, with "light" as the exception message
questions.why: `??=` is null-coalescing assignment: evaluate the left side and assign the right only if it is null. An empty string is not null, so it is left alone. It is handy for lazy initialisation such as `_cache ??= Load();`.
questions.asked: Short syntax question; mirrors JavaScript's `??=`, which helps if you come from there.

questions.q: Why do style guides prefer `if (order is null)` over `if (order == null)`?
choices: `is null` also returns true for default structs, which `== null` misses
`is null` cannot be redirected by a user-defined `==` operator on the type
`is null` checks the database value, while `== null` checks the C# value
`is null` is evaluated at compile time, so it does not cost anything at runtime
questions.why: A class can overload `==` and make `== null` do something odd or throw. The `is null` pattern always compiles to a plain reference check, and `is not null` reads naturally. For ordinary types the result is the same; the pattern form is simply guaranteed.
questions.asked: Shows you know operator overloading exists and that patterns sidestep it.

questions.q: With nullable reference types enabled, what does the `!` in `user!.Name` do at runtime?
choices: It throws an ArgumentNullException immediately if user is null
It converts a null user into a default instance before reading Name
It skips the property access and returns null if user is null
Nothing: it only silences the compiler's null warning at that spot
questions.why: The null-forgiving operator is purely a compile-time annotation; it emits no check. If `user` is null you still get a NullReferenceException on `.Name`. Use it only where you know more than the compiler, and prefer a real check or `ArgumentNullException.ThrowIfNull` otherwise.
questions.asked: People sprinkle `!` to make warnings go away; interviewers want to hear that it hides rather than fixes the problem.

questions.q: A project has `<Nullable>enable</Nullable>`. What happens when you build code that may dereference a null `string?`?
choices: The build fails with an error unless warnings-as-errors is switched off
The compiler inserts a null check that throws before the dereference
The build succeeds with a warning, unless warnings are treated as errors
Nothing at build time; the runtime logs a warning on the first null
questions.why: Nullable reference types are a static analysis layer: they produce warnings such as CS8602, not errors, and change nothing at runtime. Teams often add `<WarningsAsErrors>nullable</WarningsAsErrors>` so the warnings actually block a merge.
questions.asked: Tells an interviewer whether you have actually worked in a project with nullability on, and how you enforce it.

questions.q: What does this print?
choices: Active, because the first member is the default
0, because no member has the value zero
An empty line, because default gives null
A compile error, because 0 is not a member
questions.why: Every enum's default is the underlying value 0, whether or not a member has that value, and `ToString()` prints the number when no name matches. That is why guidance says to define a zero member such as `None` or `Unknown`, and why an unset enum property in a DTO can slip past validation.
questions.asked: A realistic bug in request models; strong answers mention defining a zero member or validating with `Enum.IsDefined`.

questions.q: A request body sets `"role": 99` for an enum `Role { User = 0, Admin = 1 }`, and it binds without error. How do you reject it?
choices: Mark the enum [Flags] so that undefined numeric values fail to bind
Nothing is needed: casting 99 to Role already throws InvalidCastException
Switch the property type to `Role?` so that out-of-range values become null
Check it with `Enum.IsDefined(role)` or a validation attribute such as [EnumDataType]
questions.why: C# lets any value of the underlying type be cast to an enum, so 99 is a perfectly valid `Role` at runtime. You have to validate explicitly: `Enum.IsDefined` (generic overload since .NET 5) or `[EnumDataType(typeof(Role))]`. Making it nullable or adding [Flags] does not restrict the range.
questions.asked: Unvalidated enum values are a classic source of odd data in CRUD apps.

questions.q: What is the `[Flags]` attribute on an enum for?
choices: It stores the enum as a string in the database instead of an integer
It marks members as powers of two that can be combined with `|`
It makes the compiler reject any value that is not a named member
It lets a variable hold only one member at a time, like a radio group
questions.why: `[Flags]` documents that the enum is a bit set, e.g. `Read = 1, Write = 2, Delete = 4`, so `Read | Write` is meaningful and `ToString()` prints "Read, Write". You still assign the power-of-two values yourself. Test membership with `perms.HasFlag(Permissions.Write)` or a bitwise `&`.
questions.asked: Permissions and feature toggles are often stored this way; you need to read it in existing code.

questions.q: What is the difference between `int.Parse(s)` and `int.TryParse(s, out var n)`?
choices: Parse returns null for bad input; TryParse throws a FormatException
Parse ignores whitespace; TryParse fails if the string has any spaces
Parse throws on bad input; TryParse returns false and sets n to 0
Parse uses the invariant culture; TryParse uses the current culture
questions.why: `Parse` throws `FormatException` (or `ArgumentNullException`, `OverflowException`) when the input is not a valid int. `TryParse` never throws for bad input: it returns a bool and puts the result, or 0, in the out variable. Use TryParse for user input where failure is expected. Both use the current culture by default.
questions.asked: The Try pattern is idiomatic C#, and it ties into the question of when exceptions are appropriate.

questions.q: What does `Console.WriteLine(Math.Round(2.5));` print by default?
questions.why: `Math.Round` defaults to `MidpointRounding.ToEven` (banker's rounding): a midpoint rounds to the nearest even number, so 2.5 gives 2 and 3.5 gives 4. For the school rule, pass `MidpointRounding.AwayFromZero`. This matters when your totals must match an invoice or a spreadsheet.
questions.asked: A real source of one-cent discrepancies in billing code; knowing the default is the whole point.

questions.q: What is the difference between `(User)obj` and `obj as User`?
choices: The cast returns null on failure; `as` throws an InvalidCastException
The cast works only on value types; `as` works only on classes
The cast runs a conversion operator; `as` copies the object's fields
The cast throws on a type mismatch; `as` yields null instead
questions.why: A direct cast throws `InvalidCastException` when `obj` is not a `User`; `as` returns null, so it only works with reference or nullable types. Modern code usually prefers `if (obj is User u)`, which tests and casts in one step and avoids a later null check.
questions.asked: Basic, but a strong answer moves straight to the `is` pattern.

questions.q: Why does `decimal price = 9.99;` fail to compile?
choices: 9.99 is a double literal, and double does not convert implicitly to decimal
decimal variables must be declared with an explicit precision, like SQL
Literals with more than one decimal place require the `new decimal()` syntax
decimal is a reference type, so it must be created with the new keyword
questions.why: An unsuffixed literal with a decimal point is a `double`. The compiler refuses an implicit double-to-decimal conversion because it could lose information, so you write `9.99m`. Likewise `f` means float and `L` means long.
questions.asked: Trivial once you know it, and a common first compile error for newcomers writing a price field.

questions.q: What does this print?
choices: 7:Ann
Id:Name
A compile error: tuples cannot be deconstructed
questions.why: `(int Id, string Name)` is a named `ValueTuple`. `var (id, name) = ...` deconstructs it by position into two locals. Tuples are handy for returning two related values from a private helper; for public APIs a record is usually clearer.
questions.asked: Tuples replace many out-parameter APIs, and interviewers like to hear when you would pick a record instead.

questions.q: What does this print?
choices: True, then True
False, then False
False, then True
True, then False
questions.why: Tuple `==` (C# 7.3+) compares element by element, so it is True. ValueTuples are structs, so `ReferenceEquals` boxes each one into a separate object and returns False. It is a reminder that reference identity is meaningless for value types.
questions.asked: Checks that value equality versus identity is clear in your head, not just memorised for classes.

questions.q: What does this print?
choices: Woof Meow
... Meow
Woof ...
questions.why: `override` replaces the virtual method, so a Dog seen as an Animal still says Woof. `new` only hides the method for callers who see the variable as `Cat`; through an `Animal` reference the virtual call reaches `Animal.Speak`. Method hiding is almost always a mistake, which is why the compiler warns without `new`.
questions.asked: Distinguishes people who understand virtual dispatch from those who think `new` and `override` are synonyms.

questions.q: In what order do the constructors run for `new Manager()` when `Manager : Employee : Person`?
choices: Manager, then Employee, then Person
Person, then Employee, then Manager
Only Manager, unless it calls base() explicitly
Employee, then Person, then Manager
questions.why: Every constructor first calls a base constructor (implicitly `base()` if you do not write one), so the chain runs down to `object` and the bodies execute from the most basic class outwards. Field initialisers are the exception: they run before the base call, in derived-to-base order.
questions.asked: Matters when a base constructor calls a virtual method that relies on derived state that is not set yet.

questions.q: When does a static constructor run?
choices: Every time a new instance of the class is created
When the application starts, before Main is called
Only when your code calls it explicitly by name
Once, just before the type is first used
questions.why: The runtime runs a static constructor at most once per type, before the first instance is created or any static member is accessed. You cannot call it or give it parameters. If it throws, the type is unusable for the rest of the process and every access raises `TypeInitializationException`.
questions.asked: A TypeInitializationException in production usually traces back to a static constructor reading bad config.

questions.q: What does this print?
choices: True True
False True
True False
False False
questions.why: `{ get; } = expr` is an initialiser: it runs once when the object is constructed and the value is stored in a backing field, so CreatedA never changes. `=> expr` is an expression-bodied getter that runs on every read, so CreatedB is 50 ms later the second time. Mixing the two up is a common bug in entities.
questions.asked: The two syntaxes differ by one character and behave completely differently; interviewers like it as a code-review question.

questions.q: What does the `init` accessor in `public string Email { get; init; }` allow?
choices: Setting Email in a constructor or object initialiser, but not afterwards
Setting Email once from anywhere, after which further assignments throw
Reading Email only after it has been explicitly initialised by a setter
Setting Email from inside the class, but never from calling code
questions.why: An `init` accessor can only be called during object construction: in a constructor, an object initialiser like `new User { Email = "a@b.c" }`, or a `with` expression. Any later assignment is a compile error, not a runtime exception. It gives immutable DTOs without long constructors.
questions.asked: Common in request/response models; explaining it well shows you understand object initialisers.

questions.q: What is the difference between a constructor and an object initialiser such as `new User { Name = "Ann" }`?
choices: An object initialiser replaces the constructor, which is then never called
An object initialiser runs before the constructor, so the constructor can see the values
The constructor runs first; the initialiser then sets accessible properties on the result
They are identical: the compiler turns initialisers into constructor parameters
questions.why: `new User { Name = "Ann" }` calls the parameterless (or named) constructor and then assigns each listed property, so the constructor cannot see those values. Validation that must see them belongs in a constructor with parameters or uses `required` members.
questions.asked: Explains why constructor-time invariants cannot rely on initialised properties.

questions.q: What does `public class Report(ILogger<Report> logger)` (a primary constructor on a class, C# 12) create?
choices: A public read-only property called Logger that holds the injected logger
A parameter that is in scope throughout the class body, but no property
A private readonly field called _logger that the compiler names for you
A record-style class with value equality and a generated Deconstruct method
questions.why: On a class, primary constructor parameters are just parameters that the whole class body can see; the compiler captures them into hidden fields only if members use them. Unlike positional records, no public properties or equality are generated, and the captured parameter is not readonly.
questions.asked: Primary constructors are now common for DI in services; people wrongly expect record behaviour.

questions.q: What does `required` on `public required string Name { get; init; }` enforce?
choices: A runtime check in the setter that throws if the assigned value is null
That Name is validated as non-empty by ASP.NET Core model binding
That the property is always serialised to JSON, even when it is null
That every object creation site sets Name, or the code will not compile
questions.why: `required` (C# 11) is a compile-time rule: `new Person()` without setting Name is an error. It does not check the value, so `Name = null!` or `Name = ""` still compiles. A constructor marked `[SetsRequiredMembers]` satisfies it. Serialisers such as System.Text.Json treat it as required on deserialisation.
questions.asked: Frequently used with nullable reference types to avoid `= null!` on DTO properties.

questions.q: What does the `field` keyword do inside a property accessor in C# 14 (.NET 10)?
choices: It refers to the compiler-generated backing field of that property
It refers to the first field declared in the enclosing class
It declares a new local variable scoped to the setter only
It marks the property as a public field for serialisers
questions.why: C# 14 lets an accessor refer to the auto-property's hidden backing field with `field`, so you can add logic to one accessor without declaring `private string _name;` by hand. The other accessor can stay auto-implemented, as `get;` does here.
questions.asked: Tests whether you are current with the language; it removes a lot of boilerplate in validated properties.

questions.q: What is the default access level of a method declared without a modifier inside a class, and of a top-level class declared without a modifier?
choices: public for the method, and public for the class
private for the method, and internal for the class
internal for the method, and public for the class
protected for the method, and internal for the class
questions.why: C# defaults to the most restrictive sensible level: members are `private`, and non-nested types are `internal` (visible within the same assembly). This is why a class your test project cannot see is usually missing `public` or `InternalsVisibleTo`.
questions.asked: A basics question that explains a very common "why can't my test see this class" problem.

questions.q: What does `private protected` allow?
choices: Access from derived classes in any assembly, and from anything in the same assembly
Access only from the declaring class and its nested types, never from subclasses
Access from derived classes, but only those in the same assembly
Access from any class in the same namespace, whatever the assembly
questions.why: `private protected` (C# 7.2) is the intersection: the caller must both derive from the type and live in the same assembly. `protected internal` is the union. Namespaces play no part in C# access control.
questions.asked: Usually asked right after `protected internal`, to see whether you understand union versus intersection.

questions.q: How is a test project usually allowed to call `internal` classes in the project under test?
choices: By adding `[assembly: InternalsVisibleTo("MyApp.Tests")]` or the MSBuild item
By putting the tests in the same namespace as the internal classes
By marking the tests with [Fact(Internal = true)] in xUnit
By referencing the project with `PrivateAssets="all"` in the csproj
questions.why: `InternalsVisibleTo` grants a named friend assembly access to internal types; modern SDK projects can declare it as `<InternalsVisibleTo Include="MyApp.Tests" />`. Namespaces do not affect access, and PrivateAssets is about transitive package flow.
questions.asked: Shows you have set up a real test project; interviewers may follow up on whether testing internals is a smell.

questions.q: What is a `static` class in C#?
choices: A class whose instances are shared across all threads automatically
A class that holds only static members and cannot be instantiated
A class whose methods are inlined by the JIT for extra speed
A class that is created once per request by the DI container
questions.why: A static class is sealed and abstract under the hood: no instances, only static members. Helper collections such as `Math` and every class that declares extension methods are static. Singleton lifetime in DI is a different idea: that is one instance of a normal class.
questions.asked: Basics; a good follow-up is why static helpers with hidden dependencies make code hard to test.

questions.q: What does `sealed` on a class do?
choices: It makes every field in the class readonly after construction
It hides the class from other assemblies, like internal
It stops any other class from inheriting from it
It prevents the class from being serialised to JSON
questions.why: A sealed class cannot be used as a base class. It communicates that the type was not designed for extension and lets the JIT devirtualise calls. On a method, `sealed override` stops further overriding in subclasses.
questions.asked: Asked to see whether you think about designing for inheritance; many teams seal classes by default.

questions.q: What is a `partial` class used for in modern .NET code?
choices: Splitting one class across files, often so a source generator can add members
Declaring a class that is only partly implemented, like an abstract class
Letting a class inherit from two base classes, one per partial file
Loading half of a class lazily the first time one of its members is used
questions.why: All `partial` declarations are merged into one type at compile time. Today that mostly serves source generators: `[GeneratedRegex]`, `[LoggerMessage]` and System.Text.Json's `JsonSerializerContext` all need a partial type or method for the generator to fill in. It does not change inheritance rules.
questions.asked: Knowing why generators need partial shows you have used them rather than just heard of them.

questions.q: What is the difference between an optional parameter and a named argument?
questions.code:
void Send(string to, bool urgent = false, int retries = 3) { }

Send("ann@x.io", retries: 5);
choices: Optional parameters must be named at the call site, or the code will not compile
The declaration gives defaults; the call names the argument, skipping `urgent`
Named arguments are only allowed when every earlier parameter is also named
Optional parameters are resolved at runtime, so changing a default needs no rebuild
questions.why: `urgent = false` declares a default so callers may omit it; `retries: 5` names the argument so you can skip `urgent` and still set the third one. Like const, default values are baked into the caller at compile time, so changing one in a library needs callers to recompile.
questions.asked: Everyday syntax; the versioning detail about defaults being compiled into callers is what impresses.

questions.q: What does `nameof(order.CustomerId)` evaluate to?
choices: The value of order.CustomerId, converted to a string
The fully qualified name "Shop.Order.CustomerId"
The string "CustomerId", fixed at compile time
The string "order.CustomerId", including the variable
questions.why: `nameof` produces the simple name of the symbol as a compile-time constant, so it survives renames. It is standard in `ArgumentException(nameof(x))`, `PropertyChanged` and log messages. It does not evaluate the expression or include the qualifier.
questions.asked: Small, but it signals you write refactor-safe code.

questions.q: What does a file-scoped namespace, `namespace Shop.Orders;`, change compared with the braced form?
choices: It limits every type in the file to internal visibility
It creates a namespace that exists only while that file compiles
It applies the namespace to the whole file without an extra level of indentation
It lets the file declare types in several namespaces at once
questions.why: File-scoped namespaces (C# 10) are pure syntax: everything in the file belongs to that namespace, and you lose one level of nesting. A file can have only one. Accessibility is unchanged.
questions.asked: Shows familiarity with the modern templates, which all use this form.

questions.q: In a .NET 9 project with `<ImplicitUsings>enable</ImplicitUsings>`, why does `List<T>` work without a `using System.Collections.Generic;` line?
choices: The SDK generates global using directives for common namespaces
The compiler searches every referenced namespace for unknown types
List<T> was moved into the System namespace in .NET 6
Visual Studio adds the usings when it opens the file
questions.why: The SDK writes a generated `GlobalUsings.g.cs` with `global using System.Collections.Generic;` and friends, chosen per project type (web projects add ASP.NET Core namespaces). You can add your own `global using` lines or `<Using Include=...>` items.
questions.asked: Newcomers are confused by code that compiles without usings; being able to explain it is basic literacy.

questions.q: In a Program.cs with top-level statements, what does the compiler generate?
choices: A static class named App with an instance Run method
A Program class with a Main method wrapping those statements
A script that is interpreted at runtime without compilation
A Startup class whose Configure method holds the statements
questions.why: Top-level statements are sugar for an entry point: the compiler emits a `Program` class with a `Main` (async if you use await) containing your statements. Only one file per project may have them. This is why integration tests can reference `Program` via `public partial class Program { }`.
questions.asked: Links the minimal hosting template to what actually runs, and to the WebApplicationFactory<Program> trick.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.code:
var price = 1234.5m;
Console.WriteLine($"{price:N2}|{price,10:F1}|{42:D5}");
choices: A FormatException, since D only applies to decimal
questions.why: `N2` adds group separators and two decimals; `,10` right-aligns in a 10-character field and `F1` gives one decimal; `D5` pads an integer with leading zeros. `D` is for integer types only, so it is fine on 42. Formatting uses the current culture, so the separators vary by locale.
questions.asked: Format strings turn up in reports, CSV exports and emails; knowing they are culture-sensitive is the real point.

questions.q: On a server whose current culture is `de-DE`, what does `double.Parse("1.5")` return?
choices: 1.5, because parsing always uses the invariant culture
15, because '.' is the thousands separator in German
A FormatException, because German expects a comma
1, because parsing stops at the first unknown character
questions.why: `double.Parse` uses the current culture and allows thousands separators, and in de-DE `.` groups digits while `,` is the decimal point, so "1.5" silently becomes 15. For machine-readable input pass `CultureInfo.InvariantCulture`. Silent misreads like this are worse than an exception.
questions.asked: A real production bug when containers or servers run with a non-English locale; strong answers always parse data with the invariant culture.

questions.q: What does the `@` in `var path = @"C:\logs\new";` do?
choices: It interpolates variables into the string, like the $ prefix
It makes the string a UTF-8 byte array instead of UTF-16
It makes a verbatim string, so backslashes are not escapes
It interns the string so equal literals share one instance
questions.why: A verbatim string treats backslashes literally and can span lines; a double quote is written as `""`. Without `@`, `\n` in "new" would be a newline. It combines with interpolation as `$@"..."`. The `u8` suffix is what produces UTF-8 bytes.
questions.asked: Basic syntax you meet in file paths and regexes.

questions.q: What is the main advantage of a raw string literal (C# 11), written with three or more double quotes?
choices: Its content is validated as JSON by the compiler
It is stored as UTF-8, halving the memory it uses
Quotes and backslashes need no escaping, and indentation is trimmed
It is immutable, unlike ordinary string literals
questions.why: Raw string literals take their content verbatim: no escaping of quotes or backslashes, and the whitespace to the left of the closing delimiter is removed from every line. That makes embedded JSON, SQL and test fixtures readable. All string literals are immutable and UTF-16.
questions.asked: Common in tests with JSON payloads; recognising the syntax avoids confusion in code review.

questions.q: Why prefer `string.Equals(a, b, StringComparison.OrdinalIgnoreCase)` to `a.ToLower() == b.ToLower()`?
choices: ToLower throws on non-ASCII characters, while Equals handles all of Unicode
The ToLower version is case-sensitive, so it does not actually work
OrdinalIgnoreCase sorts the strings first, which makes the comparison stable
It allocates no new strings and avoids culture quirks such as the Turkish i
questions.why: `ToLower()` allocates two new strings and uses the current culture: in tr-TR, "I".ToLower() is a dotless ı, so "ID" and "id" stop matching. An ordinal ignore-case comparison needs no allocation and gives the same answer everywhere, which is what identifiers, emails and keys need.
questions.asked: The Turkish-i problem is a classic; interviewers use it to see if you think about culture at all.

questions.q: How do you make a `Dictionary<string, User>` treat "ANN" and "ann" as the same key?
choices: Override GetHashCode on string in a partial class
Call ToLower on each key when enumerating the dictionary
Construct it with `StringComparer.OrdinalIgnoreCase`
Set the dictionary's `CaseSensitive` property to false
questions.why: Dictionaries and HashSets accept an `IEqualityComparer<T>`; `new Dictionary<string, User>(StringComparer.OrdinalIgnoreCase)` hashes and compares keys case-insensitively. There is no CaseSensitive property, and lower-casing only at read time leaves duplicate keys in the store.
questions.asked: A small but practical question for lookups by username or email.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.why: Splitting "a,,b," on commas gives "a", "", "b" and a trailing "", four entries. `RemoveEmptyEntries` drops the empty ones, leaving two. Add `TrimEntries` (since .NET 5) to trim whitespace as well, which is common when parsing CSV-ish config values.
questions.asked: Parsing comma-separated query strings and config values is everyday work.

questions.q: What does this print?
choices: -004 and ORD-
0042 and ORD
0042 and ORD-
2026 and ORD
questions.why: `^4` means four from the end, and a range's end is exclusive, so `[^4..]` is the last four characters and `[..3]` is indices 0 to 2. Ranges on strings call `Substring`, so they allocate; on a span they do not.
questions.asked: Ranges and indices are modern syntax that replaces fiddly Substring arithmetic.

questions.q: What does this print?
choices: Ann nullLee twice, then an exception
Ann Lee twice, then 0
An exception on the first line, because middle is null
Ann Lee twice, then a NullReferenceException
questions.why: String concatenation and interpolation both treat null as an empty string, so the first two lines print `Ann Lee`. Calling a member on the null reference is different: `middle.Length` throws NullReferenceException (and the compiler warns with nullability on). JavaScript would print `null` in the first two.
questions.asked: Helps explain why a missing value quietly vanishes from generated text rather than crashing.

questions.q: What does `char c = 'a'; Console.WriteLine(c + 1);` print?
choices: b
a1
A compile error: cannot add int to char
questions.why: `char` is a 16-bit numeric type; `c + 1` promotes it to `int`, and 'a' is 97, so it prints 98. Cast back with `(char)(c + 1)` to get 'b'. Concatenation only happens when one operand is a string.
questions.asked: Distinguishes char from string, a common confusion coming from JavaScript where both are strings.

questions.q: What is the difference between `string.IsNullOrEmpty` and `string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace`?
choices: IsNullOrEmpty also trims the string before checking its length
IsNullOrWhiteSpace also returns true for strings made only of spaces, tabs or newlines
IsNullOrWhiteSpace returns false for null, unlike IsNullOrEmpty
IsNullOrEmpty is culture-aware, while IsNullOrWhiteSpace is ordinal
questions.why: `IsNullOrEmpty` is true for null or "". `IsNullOrWhiteSpace` is also true for "   " or "\t\n", which is usually what you want for required text fields. Both handle null safely and neither allocates.
questions.asked: A validation basic; picking IsNullOrWhiteSpace for user input shows care.

questions.q: Which statement about the C# `switch` statement is correct?
choices: Execution falls through to the next case unless you write break
Only int and enum values can be used in case labels
A case with statements must end in break, return, throw or goto
Each case must declare a new scope with braces, or the code will not compile
questions.why: C# forbids implicit fall-through from a case that contains statements (CS0163), which removes a classic C bug; stacked empty labels (`case 1: case 2:`) are still allowed. Switch works on strings, types and patterns, and braces are optional.
questions.asked: JavaScript developers expect fall-through; this checks you know C# is stricter.

questions.q: What does this print?
choices: small
medium
large
invalid
questions.why: Relational patterns with `and` build ranges, and arms are tested top to bottom. 100 fails `< 100` in the second arm and matches `>= 100 and < 1000`. The `_` discard catches everything else, which also keeps the switch expression exhaustive.
questions.asked: Business rules like pricing tiers are the everyday use of switch expressions.

questions.q: What happens here?
questions.code:
var stock = new Dictionary<string, int> { ["apple"] = 3 };
Console.WriteLine(stock["pear"]);
choices: It prints 0, the default value for int
It prints an empty line, because the key is missing
It throws KeyNotFoundException
It throws NullReferenceException
questions.why: The dictionary indexer throws `KeyNotFoundException` for a missing key, unlike a JavaScript object that returns undefined. Use `TryGetValue(key, out var n)` or `GetValueOrDefault(key)` when absence is normal.
questions.asked: The most common dictionary exception in logs; the follow-up is which API you use instead.

questions.q: What is the difference between `dict.Add(key, value)` and `dict[key] = value` when the key already exists?
choices: Add overwrites silently; the indexer throws an ArgumentException
Add throws an ArgumentException; the indexer overwrites the value
Each overwrites the old value, and Add also returns the replaced value
Each throws an exception, unless the dictionary has a custom comparer
questions.why: `Add` refuses duplicates with `ArgumentException` ("An item with the same key has already been added"), which is useful when a duplicate means a bug. The indexer setter is an upsert. `TryAdd` returns false instead of throwing.
questions.asked: Picking between Add, TryAdd and the indexer says something about how you think about duplicates.

questions.q: What happens when this runs?
choices: It removes 2 and 4, leaving [1, 3]
It removes only 2, because the loop skips the element after a removal
It throws InvalidOperationException because the collection was modified
It does not compile, because foreach variables are read-only
questions.why: `List<T>` tracks a version number, and its enumerator throws `InvalidOperationException` on the next `MoveNext` after the list changes. Use `ids.RemoveAll(id => id % 2 == 0)`, loop backwards with a `for`, or iterate over a copy.
questions.asked: Everyone hits it once; interviewers want the idiomatic fix, `RemoveAll`.

questions.q: Your service method returns a list that callers must not change. Which return type communicates that best?
choices: `List<Order>`, so callers get the fastest concrete type
`Order[]`, because arrays cannot be modified once returned
`IEnumerable<Order>`, so the caller can enumerate it more than once cheaply
`IReadOnlyList<Order>`, which gives Count and indexing but no Add
questions.why: `IReadOnlyList<T>` exposes `Count` and an indexer without mutators, and `List<T>` implements it, so there is no copy. Arrays are fixed-size but their elements are still writable. `IEnumerable<T>` hides Count and invites multiple enumeration of something that may be lazy.
questions.asked: Return types are part of an API contract; strong answers mention that a cast back to List is still possible, so use ImmutableArray when it truly matters.

questions.q: What does this print?
choices: 1, because HashSet compares the Name property of each tag
0, because both tags are equal and cancel each other out
A compile error, because Tag has no GetHashCode override
2, because a class uses reference equality by default
questions.why: HashSet asks `GetHashCode` and `Equals`, and a plain class inherits reference-based versions from `object`, so two separate instances are two items. Declare `record Tag(string Name)`, override both methods, or pass an `IEqualityComparer<Tag>`.
questions.asked: Shows you understand what hashing collections actually rely on.

questions.q: You override `Equals` on a class but not `GetHashCode`. What goes wrong?
choices: Equal objects can land in different hash buckets, so Dictionary and HashSet miss them
Nothing at runtime: GetHashCode is only used by the debugger
Every call to == now throws, because the two methods disagree
The class can no longer be serialised to JSON
questions.why: Hash-based collections find the bucket via `GetHashCode` before calling `Equals`. If equal objects return different hash codes, a lookup searches the wrong bucket and fails. The rule is: equal objects must have equal hash codes; `HashCode.Combine(a, b)` makes that easy. The compiler warns (CS0659) for exactly this reason.
questions.asked: A standard contract question; the HashCode.Combine detail shows you have done it recently.

questions.q: A `User` object is used as a dictionary key, and its hash code is based on `Email`. What happens after you change the user's Email?
choices: The dictionary re-hashes the entry automatically on the next lookup
Lookups by that object will usually fail, although it is still in the dictionary
The dictionary throws InvalidOperationException on the next access
The entry is removed from the dictionary when the property changes
questions.why: The entry was filed under the old hash code. After the change, `ContainsKey(user)` hashes to a different bucket and misses it, yet enumeration still shows it. Keys must be immutable, or at least their hashed fields must be; use an ID or a record with init-only properties.
questions.asked: Explains a baffling bug class; strong answers say "hash only immutable fields".

questions.q: What is iteration order of a `Dictionary<TKey, TValue>` in .NET?
choices: Always insertion order, which the documentation guarantees
Always sorted by key, because entries are stored in a tree
Always reversed insertion order, like a stack
Undefined: it often looks like insertion order but you cannot rely on it
questions.why: The implementation happens to return insertion order until you remove items, after which freed slots are reused and the order changes. The docs call the order unspecified. Use `SortedDictionary` for key order or keep a separate list, or `OrderedDictionary<TKey, TValue>` (generic since .NET 9) for guaranteed insertion order.
questions.asked: People ship code that depends on the accidental order; this checks you know it is not a contract.

questions.q: Which collection suits a work queue that must always hand out the job with the lowest priority number first?
choices: `PriorityQueue<TElement, TPriority>`
`Queue<T>`, sorted after each Enqueue
`SortedList<TKey, TValue>` keyed by priority
`Stack<T>` with the lowest items pushed last
questions.why: `PriorityQueue<TElement, TPriority>` (.NET 6) is a min-heap: `Enqueue(job, priority)` and `Dequeue()` return the smallest priority in O(log n). A SortedList keyed by priority cannot hold two jobs with the same priority, and re-sorting a Queue is O(n log n) every time.
questions.asked: Picking the right collection is a practical skill; interviewers like hearing the duplicate-key flaw in SortedList.

questions.q: When is `FrozenDictionary<TKey, TValue>` (.NET 8) the right choice?
choices: When many threads write to the dictionary concurrently
When the data is built once at startup and then only read
When you need entries kept in insertion order
When keys expire automatically after a timeout
questions.why: `ToFrozenDictionary()` spends extra time at creation to build a lookup structure optimised for reads, and the result can never change. It suits configuration, lookup tables and routing maps. Concurrent writes need `ConcurrentDictionary`; expiry needs a cache such as `IMemoryCache`.
questions.asked: A modern-.NET awareness question; the trade-off (slow build, fast reads, immutable) is the answer they want.

questions.q: `list.Contains(x)` is in a hot loop over 50,000 items and profiling shows it dominates. What is the usual fix?
choices: Sort the list first, so Contains can stop early
Replace the List<T> with an array, which has a faster Contains
Put the items in a HashSet<T> once and call Contains on that
Call Contains through LINQ, which caches previous results
questions.why: `List<T>.Contains` is a linear scan, so 50,000 lookups against 50,000 items is billions of comparisons. Building a `HashSet<T>` once makes each lookup O(1) on average. Sorting does not change List.Contains, and LINQ's Contains on a list just calls the same method.
questions.asked: The single most common performance fix in business code; interviewers like a quick, confident answer.

questions.q: What is the difference between `Select` and `SelectMany`?
choices: x has 3 strings and y has 2 arrays
x and y both have 3 strings; SelectMany is just faster
x has 2 arrays and y has 3 strings
x has 2 arrays and y has 2 flattened arrays
questions.why: `Select` maps each element to one result, so x is a sequence of two arrays. `SelectMany` maps each element to a sequence and flattens them, like JavaScript's `flatMap`, so y is "a", "b", "c". It is how you get every order line across a list of orders.
questions.asked: A LINQ basics question; mapping it to flatMap helps JavaScript developers.

questions.q: What does this print?
choices: Bob,Ann,Cy
Ann,Cy,Bob
Cy,Bob,Ann
Ann,Bob,Cy
questions.why: A second `OrderBy` starts a new primary sort, so the result is simply ordered by name: Ann, Bob, Cy. To sort by age and then by name you need `OrderBy(p => p.Item2).ThenBy(p => p.Item1)`, which would give Bob, Ann, Cy.
questions.asked: A classic sorting bug; `ThenBy` is the expected fix.

questions.q: What does `ToDictionary` do if two elements produce the same key?
questions.code: var byEmail = users.ToDictionary(u => u.Email);
choices: It keeps the last element with that key
It throws ArgumentException
It keeps the first element with that key
It groups them into a list under the key
questions.why: `ToDictionary` calls `Add` for each element, so a duplicate key throws `ArgumentException`. If duplicates are possible, use `ToLookup` or `GroupBy`, or deduplicate first with `DistinctBy`. JavaScript's `Object.fromEntries` silently keeps the last one, which is why this surprises people.
questions.asked: Real production crashes come from assuming a column is unique; interviewers like the ToLookup alternative.

questions.q: What does this print?
choices: UK=17 FR=5
FR=5 UK=17
UK=10 FR=5 UK=7
UK=2 FR=1
questions.why: LINQ-to-objects `GroupBy` yields each group in the order its key first appears, and each group is an `IGrouping<TKey, TElement>` you can aggregate. So UK comes first with 10 + 7. Unlike SQL, grouping does not sort.
questions.asked: Grouping and summing is daily reporting work; knowing the order guarantee avoids needless OrderBy.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.why: `Distinct` uses the default equality comparer, which for a plain class is reference equality, so two instances survive. `DistinctBy` (.NET 6) compares the selected key, so only one remains. A record, or an `IEqualityComparer<Item>`, would make plain Distinct work.
questions.asked: Ties LINQ to equality semantics, which interviewers like to probe from different angles.

questions.q: What happens here?
choices: 0, then 0, because an empty average is defined as zero
0, then an InvalidOperationException
An InvalidOperationException on the first line, from Sum
0, then NaN, because the average divides zero by zero
questions.why: `Sum` of an empty sequence is 0, the natural identity. `Average`, `Min` and `Max` have no sensible answer for an empty non-nullable sequence, so they throw "Sequence contains no elements". Guard with `Any()`, use `DefaultIfEmpty()`, or project to `decimal?` so they return null.
questions.asked: Reports with no data yet crash on exactly this; the nullable-projection trick is a strong answer.

questions.q: What does `new List<int>().All(x => x > 100)` return?
choices: true, because no element breaks the rule
false, because there are no elements to check
null, because the sequence is empty
It throws InvalidOperationException
questions.why: `All` is vacuously true for an empty sequence: it returns false only when it finds a counterexample. `Any(predicate)` on an empty sequence is false. It matters in checks like "all line items shipped" on an order that has no lines.
questions.asked: Logic edge case that causes real bugs in status calculations.

questions.q: What is the difference between `Cast<T>()` and `OfType<T>()` on a mixed `IEnumerable`?
choices: Cast<T> skips elements of the wrong type; OfType<T> throws on them
Cast<T> converts numbers, e.g. int to long; OfType<T> does not
Cast<T> throws on an element of the wrong type; OfType<T> skips it
Cast<T> runs immediately; OfType<T> is deferred until enumeration
questions.why: Both are deferred. `Cast<T>` does a reference/unboxing cast per element and throws `InvalidCastException` on a mismatch; `OfType<T>` filters to matching elements. Neither performs numeric conversions, so casting boxed ints to long throws.
questions.asked: Filtering heterogeneous collections, such as domain events by type, uses OfType.

questions.q: Which call runs the query immediately rather than deferring it?
choices: `orders.Where(o => o.Paid)`
`orders.Select(o => o.Total)`
`orders.OrderBy(o => o.Date)`
`orders.ToLookup(o => o.CustomerId)`
questions.why: `ToLookup`, like `ToList`, `ToArray`, `ToDictionary`, `Count` and `First`, enumerates the source straight away and stores the result. `Where`, `Select` and `OrderBy` only build a pipeline that runs when enumerated. `GroupBy` is deferred, but `ToLookup` is its eager twin.
questions.asked: Knowing which operators are eager lets you reason about when a database or file is actually hit.

questions.q: Which statement about query syntax (`from o in orders where o.Paid select o`) is true?
choices: It runs faster, because the compiler turns it into a for loop
It is translated into the same Where/Select method calls by the compiler
It works only against databases, while method syntax works in memory
It supports every LINQ operator, including Take and Distinct, as keywords
