questions.why: Query expressions are syntactic sugar: the compiler rewrites them into calls such as `Where` and `Select`, so performance is identical. Operators with no keyword, like `Take`, `Distinct` or `Count`, need method syntax. Query syntax is mostly preferred for joins and `let`.
questions.asked: Reading older codebases requires both forms; knowing they compile to the same thing is the point.

questions.q: A method takes `IEnumerable<Order> orders` and calls `orders.Count()` and then `foreach (var o in orders)`. Why do analysers warn about this?
choices: Count() on IEnumerable always throws when the source is a List
foreach cannot be used on a sequence after Count() has been called
Count() moves the enumerator to the end, so the loop sees no items
If orders is a lazy query, it is executed twice, repeating any work or I/O
questions.why: An `IEnumerable<T>` might be a deferred query or iterator; each enumeration reruns it, which can mean two database queries or a different result the second time. Materialise once with `ToList()`, or accept `IReadOnlyCollection<T>` if you need the count. Each enumeration gets a fresh enumerator, so the loop is not empty.
questions.asked: The "possible multiple enumeration" warning is everywhere; explaining why it matters shows real understanding.

questions.q: What does `finally` guarantee here?
choices: cleanup is never printed, because return exits the method first
cleanup is printed only if an exception is thrown in the try
cleanup is printed before the method returns 1 to its caller
The code does not compile: a try with return cannot have a finally
questions.why: A `finally` block runs whenever control leaves the try, whether by falling off the end, `return`, or an exception. The return value is computed first, then finally runs, then the method returns. It does not run if the process is killed.
questions.asked: Basics of cleanup, and the reason `using` works.

questions.q: What does the `when` clause add in this catch?
choices: It catches the exception and then rethrows it if the condition is false
It runs the condition after the catch body, to decide whether to log
It makes the catch apply to every exception type that has a StatusCode
It catches only when the condition is true; otherwise the exception passes on untouched
questions.why: An exception filter is evaluated before the stack unwinds. If it is false, the catch is skipped as though it did not exist, so the original stack trace is intact and outer handlers see it. That is cleaner than catching, testing and `throw;`.
questions.asked: Filters are idiomatic modern C#; a strong answer mentions that the stack is not unwound.

questions.q: Why does this fail to compile?
choices: Only one catch block is allowed per try statement
The IOException catch is unreachable, because Exception already catches it
IOException must be caught with a `when` filter, not a plain catch
The variable name ex is declared twice in the same scope
questions.why: Catch clauses are tried in order, and a clause for a base type makes a later clause for a derived type unreachable, so the compiler reports CS0160. Order catches from most specific to most general. Each catch has its own scope, so reusing `ex` is fine.
questions.asked: Basic, but tells the interviewer you know the catch order rule.

questions.q: What is the idiomatic guard at the top of a public method in .NET 8+?
choices: `if (order == null) return;` at the start of the method, once for every parameter
`Debug.Assert(order != null);` at the start of the method, once for every parameter
`ArgumentNullException.ThrowIfNull(order);` then `ArgumentException.ThrowIfNullOrEmpty(carrier);`
`order ??= new Order();` and `carrier ??= "";` so the method always has usable values
questions.why: The throw helpers throw the correct exception with the parameter name filled in via `CallerArgumentExpression`, in one line each. Silently returning hides bugs, `Debug.Assert` vanishes in release builds, and inventing a default object corrupts data.
questions.asked: Shows you write defensive public APIs using the current helpers.

questions.q: What does this print?
choices: first
second
first, then second on the next line
One or more errors occurred. (first) (second)
questions.why: When a `finally` block throws while another exception is propagating, the new exception replaces the original, which is lost entirely. That is why cleanup code (including `Dispose`) should not throw, and why a failing Dispose can hide the real error in your logs.
questions.asked: Explains logs that show a cleanup error while the root cause vanished.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.why: A lambda captures the variable, not its value. A `for` loop has one `i` shared by all iterations, so all three closures see its final value, 3. `foreach` gets a fresh variable per iteration (since C# 5), so the same code with foreach prints 012. Copy to a local inside the loop to fix it.
questions.asked: Closure capture is identical to JavaScript's `var` in loops; interviewers use it to test understanding of captured variables.

questions.q: What does the `event` keyword add to a delegate field?
questions.code: public event EventHandler<OrderPlaced>? Placed;
choices: Outside code can only `+=` and `-=`; only the owning class can invoke or reset it
The handlers are run on a background thread, so raising it never blocks
Handlers are held with weak references, so subscribers never leak
Each subscriber receives its own copy of the event arguments
questions.why: Without `event`, any caller could do `Placed = null` and wipe other subscribers, or invoke it directly. The keyword restricts outsiders to adding and removing handlers. Handlers still run synchronously on the raising thread, and the publisher holds strong references, which is the classic event memory leak.
questions.asked: Shows you know what encapsulation events give over a public delegate field, and the leak it does not solve.

questions.q: What does this print?
choices: 1, 2 and 3 on separate lines
questions.why: Delegates are multicast: `+=` builds an invocation list and calling it runs every target in order. For a delegate with a return value you only get the last target's result; the earlier ones are discarded. That is why event handlers return void and use event args to pass data back.
questions.asked: Deep delegate knowledge; it explains why returning values from events is an anti-pattern.

questions.q: When does `ArgumentNullException` get thrown here?
choices: At line A, when Upper is called with null
At line B, when the loop first calls MoveNext
Never, because iterators ignore null sources
At compile time, because of the null! literal
questions.why: An iterator method's whole body, guard included, runs lazily on the first `MoveNext`, so the error surfaces far from the bad call. The fix is a non-iterator wrapper that validates and then returns a private iterator (or a local function). LINQ's own operators are written that way.
questions.asked: Explains confusing stack traces from lazy code and shows you know how LINQ validates eagerly.

questions.q: What is needed for a type to be usable in a `foreach` loop?
choices: It must implement IEnumerable or IEnumerable<T>, with no exceptions
It must be an array, a List<T> or a type deriving from Collection<T>
It must expose a public Count property and an int indexer
It needs an accessible GetEnumerator() returning a type with MoveNext() and Current
questions.why: foreach is pattern-based: the compiler looks for a `GetEnumerator()` method (instance or, since C# 9, extension) whose result has `MoveNext()` and `Current`. Implementing IEnumerable<T> is the usual way to provide it, which is how `List<T>` avoids allocating by returning a struct enumerator.
questions.asked: Tests whether you know the compiler relies on patterns, which also explains await and using behaviour.

questions.q: In what order are `a` and `b` disposed?
choices: a then b, in the order they were declared
b then a, in reverse order of declaration
In an unspecified order chosen by the garbage collector
Neither: using declarations dispose only on exceptions
questions.why: Using declarations are disposed at the end of the enclosing scope in reverse order, exactly like nested using blocks. That matters when b depends on a, e.g. a command that uses a connection. Disposal is deterministic; the GC is not involved.
questions.asked: Resource ordering matters with connections, transactions and streams.

questions.q: A class implements `IAsyncDisposable` because it must flush a buffer over the network. How should a caller use it?
choices: `using var w = new Writer();` which awaits DisposeAsync automatically
Call `w.DisposeAsync()` from a finalizer so it always runs
`await using var w = new Writer();` so DisposeAsync is awaited at scope end
Wrap it in `Task.Run(() => w.Dispose())` to avoid blocking
questions.why: `await using` calls and awaits `DisposeAsync()` when the scope ends, so asynchronous cleanup does not block a thread. A plain `using` needs `IDisposable` and would not compile if only `IAsyncDisposable` is implemented. Finalizers cannot await and should never do I/O.
questions.asked: Seen with streams, DbContext and HTTP writers; a strong answer mentions DI containers also call DisposeAsync.

questions.q: You forget to call `Dispose()` on a `FileStream`. What happens?
choices: The garbage collector calls Dispose as soon as the variable goes out of scope
The compiler reports an error for any IDisposable that is never disposed
The file handle stays open until a finalizer runs at some unknown later time
The runtime closes the handle when the method returns, just like using
questions.why: The GC does not call `Dispose`. FileStream's underlying SafeHandle has a finalizer that eventually releases the OS handle, but only after a garbage collection notices it, which could be much later; meanwhile the file stays locked. Deterministic cleanup is exactly what `using` is for. Analysers such as CA2000 can warn, but the compiler does not.
questions.asked: Explains "file in use" errors and why `using` is not optional.

questions.q: What does a .NET garbage collection actually decide?
choices: Which objects are no longer reachable from roots such as statics and stack locals
Which objects have not been accessed for longer than the idle timeout
Which objects have a reference count of zero, freeing them immediately
Which objects implement IDisposable and have not yet been disposed
questions.why: The .NET GC is a tracing, generational collector: it marks everything reachable from roots and reclaims the rest, so circular references are not a problem. There is no reference counting and no idle timeout, and disposal is unrelated to collection. Most objects die young in generation 0, which is cheap to collect.
questions.asked: A fundamentals question; interviewers look for "reachability from roots" and "generations".

questions.q: Which of these is a common source of memory leaks in a long-running ASP.NET Core app?
choices: Local variables inside a controller action that holds large lists
Creating many short-lived strings while building a JSON response
Objects that are allocated inside a using block and never disposed
A singleton or static field that subscribes to events or caches objects forever
questions.why: A leak in .NET means something stays reachable. Static collections that only grow, and long-lived publishers holding event handlers of shorter-lived subscribers, keep whole object graphs alive for the life of the process. Locals and short-lived strings become unreachable when the request ends.
questions.asked: Real production issue; strong answers mention dotnet-counters or a memory dump to find the root.

questions.q: What does `static` on the lambda in `items.Select(static x => x * 2)` do?
choices: It makes the lambda a static method on the containing class, visible to other code
It caches the lambda's results, so equal inputs return the stored output
It prevents the lambda from capturing locals or `this`, so no closure is allocated
It runs the lambda once at startup and reuses the resulting value
questions.why: A `static` lambda (C# 9) is a compile-time promise that it captures nothing; accidentally referencing a local or instance member becomes an error. That guarantees no closure object allocation, which matters on hot paths. It does not memoise or change visibility.
questions.asked: Shows awareness of hidden allocations from closures in hot code.

questions.q: Why might you write a local function rather than assigning a lambda to a local `Func<>`?
choices: Local functions run on a separate thread pool thread, so they never block the calling method
They can recurse, be called above their declaration, and avoid a delegate allocation
Local functions can be passed as arguments to other methods, whereas lambdas never can
Local functions are the only way to use `yield return` from inside a lambda expression body
questions.why: A local function is a real method: it can be generic, recursive and called above its definition, and when it is not converted to a delegate its captures can live in a struct rather than a heap closure. Lambdas can be passed around just as well, and neither changes threading.
questions.asked: Comes up when reviewing helpers inside methods; the allocation detail is the deep part.

questions.q: What does this print?
choices: True, then False
False, then True
True, then True
It throws InvalidOperationException
questions.why: Arithmetic operators are lifted over nullable value types: if any operand is null the result is null, so b is null. Comparison operators return false when either side is null, so both `a > 0` and `a <= 0` are false, which breaks the usual law that one of them must hold. SQL NULL behaves in a similar way.
questions.asked: Nullable columns from a database make this real; it is a good test of careful reasoning.

questions.q: What happens at runtime?
choices: Every assignment succeeds, because the variable is typed object[]
The first line fails, because string[] cannot be converted to object[]
The last line throws ArrayTypeMismatchException
42 is converted to "42" before it is stored
questions.why: Arrays of reference types are covariant, so a `string[]` can be referenced as `object[]`, but the runtime still knows it is a string array and checks every store. Storing a boxed int throws `ArrayTypeMismatchException`. Generic interfaces like `IEnumerable<out T>` are covariant only for reading, which is why they are safe.
questions.asked: A deep type-system question that leads naturally to why List<T> is invariant.

questions.q: You sort employees by department with `list.Sort(...)` and employees with the same department change relative order. With `OrderBy` they do not. Why?
choices: List.Sort sorts by hash code first, which is effectively random
List.Sort is an unstable sort; LINQ OrderBy is a stable sort
OrderBy sorts a copy, and copying preserves the original order
List.Sort uses the current culture; OrderBy uses ordinal comparison
questions.why: `List<T>.Sort` and `Array.Sort` use introsort, which does not preserve the order of equal elements. `Enumerable.OrderBy` is documented as stable. If ties must keep a meaningful order, use OrderBy or add a tiebreaker such as ID with ThenBy.
questions.asked: Explains flickering row order in paged tables; the tiebreaker advice also applies to SQL ORDER BY.

questions.q: What is explicit interface implementation for?
choices: It makes calls to the method faster, because they skip virtual dispatch entirely
It lets subclasses override the method even though it is not marked virtual
The method is callable only via an IExportable reference, not on Order itself
It forces every class that implements the interface to supply its own ToCsv body
questions.why: An explicitly implemented member has no access modifier and is not visible on the class: `order.ToCsv()` does not compile, but `((IExportable)order).ToCsv()` does. It resolves clashes between two interfaces with the same member name, and hides members that only matter to one consumer.
questions.asked: Appears in framework code (e.g. collections implementing non-generic interfaces); knowing it helps you read them.

questions.q: What do default interface methods (C# 8) allow?
choices: Adding a member with a body to an interface without breaking existing implementers
Declaring instance fields in an interface so implementers share state
Making an interface method optional, so implementers can skip it and callers get null
Letting an interface inherit from an abstract class and reuse its methods
questions.why: A default implementation lets you evolve a published interface: existing classes inherit the body. Interfaces still cannot hold instance fields. The default is only callable through the interface type, not on the class, unless the class implements it itself.
questions.asked: Tells an interviewer whether you know how interfaces differ from abstract classes in modern C#.

questions.q: What must you implement so that `List<Money>.Sort()` works without a comparer?
choices: IEquatable<Money>, so the sort can tell when two items are equal
IComparable<Money>, whose CompareTo returns negative, zero or positive
An overloaded < operator on Money, which Sort calls directly
GetHashCode, which Sort uses to order the elements
questions.why: `Sort()` with no arguments uses `Comparer<T>.Default`, which uses `IComparable<T>`. Without it you get `InvalidOperationException` ("Failed to compare two elements"). Operators are not used by Sort, and IEquatable is for equality, not ordering.
questions.asked: Knowing IComparable versus IEquatable versus IComparer is basic framework literacy.

questions.q: Why do you implement `IEquatable<T>` on a struct used as a dictionary key?
choices: Without it, a struct cannot be used as a key at all
It lets the dictionary sort keys in addition to hashing them
It makes the struct immutable, which keys must be
It avoids the reflection-based, boxing Equals that ValueType provides
questions.why: `ValueType.Equals(object)` boxes the argument and may use reflection over the fields, which is slow in hot lookups. `EqualityComparer<T>.Default` picks up `IEquatable<T>.Equals(T)` and calls it without boxing. A `record struct` generates this for you.
questions.asked: A performance-aware question; mentioning record struct is a strong finish.

questions.q: What does this print?
choices: True True
False False
True False
False True
questions.why: Overriding `Equals` does not change the `==` operator for a class, which still compares references, so the first line is False and the second True. You must also declare `operator ==` and `operator !=`, or use a record, which generates all of them consistently.
questions.asked: Highlights why records exist: getting ==, Equals and GetHashCode consistent by hand is fiddly.

questions.q: How does `Lazy<T>` behave by default?
questions.code: private static readonly Lazy<Config> _config = new(() => LoadConfig());
choices: LoadConfig runs on first access to `.Value`, once, and is thread-safe
LoadConfig runs immediately, but on a background thread
LoadConfig runs on every access to `.Value`, returning fresh data
LoadConfig runs on first access, but may run again if two threads race
questions.why: The default mode is `LazyThreadSafetyMode.ExecutionAndPublication`: the factory runs at most once, other threads block until it finishes, and everyone gets the same value. If the factory throws, that exception is cached and rethrown on every access, which is worth knowing for config that can fail transiently.
questions.asked: Useful for expensive singletons; the cached-exception detail is what interviewers look for.

questions.q: What does C# 14 (.NET 10) add with this syntax?
choices: A way to change the behaviour of string for the whole application
A new base class for string that other classes can extend
Extension members, including extension properties like `name.IsBlank`
A pattern that matches string values inside a switch expression
questions.why: C# 14 extension blocks declare a receiver once and allow extension properties and static extension members, not just methods; callers write `name.IsBlank`. Like classic extension methods, they cannot access private state or change the type itself. Old `this`-parameter extension methods keep working.
questions.asked: A currency check on the newest language version; the answer that they are still sugar over static methods is key.

questions.q: In C# 14, what does `customer?.LastSeen = DateTime.UtcNow;` do when `customer` is null?
choices: It throws a NullReferenceException, as any assignment to null would
It creates a new customer and assigns LastSeen on it
It does nothing: the right-hand side is not evaluated and nothing is assigned
It fails to compile, because ?. is only allowed when reading a value
questions.why: C# 14 allows null-conditional member access on the left of an assignment: if customer is null the whole assignment is skipped, including evaluation of the right side. Before C# 14 this was a compile error and you wrote an `if (customer is not null)` block.
questions.asked: Recent-feature awareness; the "right side is not evaluated" detail matters when it has side effects.

questions.q: With C# 13, what can a `params` parameter be declared as?
questions.code:
static int Sum(params ReadOnlySpan<int> values) { /* ... */ return 0; }
Sum(1, 2, 3);
choices: Only an array type such as int[], exactly as it has always been in earlier versions
Any collection-expression target, such as Span<T>, ReadOnlySpan<T> or List<T>
Only IEnumerable<T>, so that the arguments are evaluated lazily by the method
Only types that implement ICollection<T> and expose a public Add method
questions.why: C# 13 params collections accept spans, `List<T>`, interfaces such as `IEnumerable<T>`, and other collection-expression targets. A `params ReadOnlySpan<int>` lets the compiler pass arguments without allocating an array, which is why many BCL methods gained span overloads.
questions.asked: Tests currency with the language and awareness of allocation-free APIs.

questions.q: Why does modern .NET code inject `TimeProvider` instead of calling `DateTime.UtcNow` directly?
choices: TimeProvider is more accurate, because it reads a hardware clock
DateTime.UtcNow is obsolete in .NET 9 and produces a warning
Tests can substitute a fake clock and control the current time and timers
TimeProvider converts every time to the user's local time zone automatically
questions.why: `TimeProvider` (.NET 8) abstracts `GetUtcNow()`, timers and delays. Production uses `TimeProvider.System`; tests use `FakeTimeProvider` from Microsoft.Extensions.TimeProvider.Testing to jump time forward, so expiry and scheduling logic can be tested without sleeps.
questions.asked: Time-dependent logic (tokens, trials, reminders) is hard to test; this is the modern answer.

questions.q: Why might you use `Guid.CreateVersion7()` (.NET 9) rather than `Guid.NewGuid()` for new primary keys?
choices: Version 7 GUIDs are shorter, which halves the index size
Version 7 GUIDs start with a timestamp, so new keys sort roughly in creation order
Version 7 GUIDs are cryptographically secure, while NewGuid is predictable
Version 7 GUIDs can be converted to an int without losing information
questions.why: `NewGuid()` creates random version 4 GUIDs, so inserts land all over a B-tree index and cause page splits. UUIDv7 puts a millisecond timestamp first, so keys are nearly sequential. Both are 128 bits. Note SQL Server orders uniqueidentifier bytes differently, so the benefit there needs care.
questions.asked: Key choice affects database performance; a strong answer mentions index fragmentation.

questions.q: Which type represents a date of birth with no time and no time zone?
choices: `DateTime` with the time part set to midnight
`DateTimeOffset` with an offset of zero
`TimeSpan` counted from 1 January 0001
`DateOnly`, added in .NET 6
questions.why: `DateOnly` holds just a calendar date, so there is no midnight-in-which-zone ambiguity that can shift a birthday by a day when converted. EF Core and System.Text.Json support it. `TimeOnly` is the matching type for opening hours.
questions.asked: Date handling bugs are common in CRUD apps; picking the precise type shows care.

questions.q: What does `default(Money)` give you for `struct Money { public decimal Amount; public string Currency; }`?
choices: Amount 0 and Currency null, whatever constructors the struct declares
Amount 0 and Currency "", because string fields default to empty
A compile error, because the struct has no parameterless constructor
Whatever values the parameterless constructor sets, if one exists
questions.why: `default(T)` for a struct is always all-bits-zero: numbers are 0 and references are null, and no constructor runs, even if you declare a parameterless one (C# 10+). Arrays of structs and uninitialised fields get the same zeroed value, which is why struct invariants cannot rely on constructors.
questions.asked: Explains how invalid structs appear, e.g. in arrays or default parameters.

questions.q: What is the difference between `IEnumerable<T>` and `IEnumerator<T>`?
choices: IEnumerable<T> is lazy, while IEnumerator<T> always holds every element in memory
IEnumerator<T> is the older non-generic form of IEnumerable<T>
IEnumerable<T> is a sequence you can iterate; IEnumerator<T> is one cursor moving through it
IEnumerable<T> is for reading, while IEnumerator<T> also allows adding elements
questions.why: `IEnumerable<T>` has one method, `GetEnumerator()`, which hands out a fresh `IEnumerator<T>` with `MoveNext()`, `Current` and `Dispose()`. Two foreach loops over the same enumerable get independent cursors. JavaScript has the same split between iterables and iterators.
questions.asked: Foundational for understanding LINQ and yield; the JS iterable analogy helps.

questions.q: What does `Enumerable.Chunk(100)` (.NET 6) return for a list of 250 ids?
choices: Three arrays with 100, 100 and 50 ids
Two arrays with 100 ids each; the last 50 are dropped
100 arrays with between 2 and 3 ids each
Three arrays padded with default values to 100 ids each
questions.why: `Chunk(size)` splits a sequence into arrays of at most `size` elements; the last chunk holds whatever is left, with no padding. It is the easy way to batch IDs for `IN (...)` queries or bulk API calls with a request-size limit.
questions.asked: Batching is a routine data-processing need; knowing Chunk saves hand-written loops.

questions.q: What does `orders.CountBy(o => o.Status)` return in .NET 9?
choices: An int with the number of distinct statuses in the sequence
A Dictionary<Status, List<Order>> built eagerly
An IEnumerable<KeyValuePair<Status, int>> with a count per status
An IGrouping<Status, Order> for the most common status
questions.why: `CountBy` (.NET 9) is a shortcut for `GroupBy(key).Select(g => new { g.Key, Count = g.Count() })` that does not build the groups: it yields `KeyValuePair<TKey, int>` entries. `AggregateBy` is its general sibling, and `Index()` gives `(int Index, T Item)` pairs.
questions.asked: Keeping up with LINQ additions shows you read release notes; CountBy is common in dashboards.

questions.q: When should a method parameter be `IList<T>` rather than `IEnumerable<T>`?
choices: Always, because IList<T> is faster to enumerate than IEnumerable<T>
When the method needs indexed access or to modify the list it is given
Never, because IList<T> cannot accept arrays
When the caller might pass a lazy LINQ query that should stay lazy
questions.why: Accept the least capable type that does the job: `IEnumerable<T>` if you only loop once, `IReadOnlyList<T>` for count and indexing, `IList<T>` if you must add, remove or set items. Arrays implement IList<T> (Add throws, since they are fixed size). A lazy query cannot be passed as IList<T> without materialising it.
questions.asked: API design question; the "least capable type" principle is what the interviewer wants to hear.

questions.q: What does this loop give you on each iteration?
choices: A copy of the dictionary, split into two parallel arrays
Each key and value, deconstructed from a KeyValuePair
Only the keys, with qty always set to its default of 0
A compile error, because a dictionary cannot be deconstructed
questions.why: Enumerating a dictionary yields `KeyValuePair<TKey, TValue>`, which has had a `Deconstruct` method since .NET Core 2.0, so `var (name, qty)` unpacks it. It is the same idea as `for (const [k, v] of Object.entries(obj))` in JavaScript.
questions.asked: Everyday syntax; mapping it to Object.entries helps JavaScript developers.
